title: Unit 10: Conductors and Capacitors

guide.title: Conductors and capacitors: review guide
guide.intro: Conductors let charge move until the field inside them vanishes. Capacitors use pairs of conductors to store charge and energy, and a dielectric between the plates lets them store more.
guide.equationNote: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²). μF = 10⁻⁶ F and pF = 10⁻¹² F.

sections.title: Electrostatics with conductors
body: In electrostatic equilibrium, the field inside a conductor is zero, any excess charge sits on its outer surface, the whole conductor is at one potential, and the field just outside is perpendicular to the surface with magnitude σ/ε₀.
A charge inside a cavity of a conductor induces an equal and opposite charge on the cavity wall, and the same amount appears on the outer surface, on top of any net charge the conductor already had.
points: Conductors joined by a wire reach the same potential; for spheres, q is proportional to R.
Charge density is highest where the surface curves most sharply.
Grounding a conductor sets its potential to zero.

sections.title: Capacitors
body: Capacitance is C = Q/ΔV. For parallel plates, C = ε₀A/d. The stored energy is U = ½QΔV = ½C(ΔV)² = Q²/(2C).
Capacitors in parallel add: C = C₁ + C₂. In series, 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂, and each capacitor holds the same charge.
points: A disconnected (isolated) capacitor keeps its charge Q when you change it.
A capacitor connected to a battery keeps its voltage ΔV.
The energy is stored in the field, with energy density u = ½ε₀E².

sections.title: Dielectrics
body: An insulating material (a dielectric) between the plates becomes polarized: its molecules' charges shift slightly, making a field that partly cancels the plates' field. That lets the capacitor hold more charge at the same voltage.
Filling the gap with a dielectric of constant κ multiplies the capacitance by κ: C = κε₀A/d.
points: Isolated capacitor plus dielectric: Q stays fixed and C grows by κ, so ΔV and E fall by a factor of κ.
Capacitor on a battery plus dielectric: ΔV stays fixed, so Q grows by κ.
κ = 1 for a vacuum and is greater than 1 for every other material.

example.prompt: A 4.0 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V and disconnected. The gap is then filled with a dielectric with κ = 2. Find the new capacitance, voltage, and stored energy.
example.solution: Q = CΔV = 40 μC stays fixed. C becomes 8.0 μF, so ΔV = Q/C = 5.0 V. U = ½QΔV = ½(40 × 10⁻⁶)(5.0) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ J, half the original 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ J; the field does work pulling the dielectric in.

misconceptions: “Excess charge spreads through a conductor's volume.”
It sits on the surface; the interior stays neutral and field-free.
“Capacitors in series add like resistors in series.”
It's the reverse: capacitors in parallel add.
“A dielectric conducts charge between the plates.”
It is an insulator; it only polarizes.
“A capacitor's energy depends only on its capacitance.”
It also depends on its charge or voltage, and whether Q or ΔV stays fixed decides how it changes.

questions.prompt: A solid metal sphere carries excess charge and is in electrostatic equilibrium. What is the electric field inside the metal?
choices: Zero, and the excess charge is spread evenly through the volume
Zero, and the excess charge sits on the outer surface
questions.explanation: If there were a field inside, the free charges would keep moving. In equilibrium the field inside the metal is zero, and the excess charge pushes itself out to the surface.
choiceExplanations: kQ/r² describes the field outside the sphere, not inside the metal.
In a conductor the excess charge moves to the surface; spread through the volume would make a field inside.
Any field inside would move charges, so equilibrium requires no field there.

questions.prompt: A thick, hollow conducting shell carries net charge +Q. A point charge +q is placed at the center of its cavity, not touching it. What charge ends up on the shell's inner and outer surfaces?
choices: Inner surface −q; outer surface Q + q
Inner surface +q; outer surface Q − q
questions.explanation: The field inside the metal must be zero, so a Gaussian surface within the metal must enclose zero net charge: the inner surface carries −q. The shell's total is +Q, so the outer surface carries Q − (−q) = Q + q.
choiceExplanations: With no charge on the inner surface, the field from +q would reach into the metal.
The inner surface responds to the charge in the cavity, q, not to the shell's own charge Q.
The induced charge on the inner surface is opposite in sign to q.

questions.prompt: Two separated conducting spheres, of radii R and 2R, are connected by a long thin wire and share a total charge Q. Which sphere has the greater surface charge density?
choices: They have equal surface charge densities
The larger sphere, because it holds more charge
The smaller sphere, with four times the larger sphere's density
The smaller sphere, with twice the larger sphere's density
questions.explanation: Connected spheres are at the same potential: kq₁/R = kq₂/(2R), so q₂ = 2q₁, giving q₁ = Q/3 and q₂ = 2Q/3. Densities: σ₁ = (Q/3)/(4πR²) and σ₂ = (2Q/3)/(16πR²) = (Q/6)/(4πR²). The smaller sphere's density is twice as large.
choiceExplanations: Equal potentials, not equal densities, are what the wire enforces.
The larger sphere holds more charge, but over four times the area, so its density is lower.
Density goes as q/R², and q ∝ R, so σ ∝ 1/R: a factor of 2, not 4.

questions.prompt: A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 1.0 mm of air. What is its capacitance? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²))
choiceExplanations: 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ multiplies by d instead of dividing.
1.8 × 10⁻¹³ uses 1.0 m for the gap instead of 1.0 mm.
4.4 × 10⁻¹³ uses d/A instead of A/d.

questions.prompt: A 3.0 μF capacitor and a 6.0 μF capacitor are connected in series. What is their equivalent capacitance?
questions.explanation: In series, 1/C = 1/3.0 + 1/6.0 = 1/2.0, so C = 2.0 μF, less than either capacitor.
choiceExplanations: 9.0 μF adds them, which is the rule for capacitors in parallel.
4.5 μF is their average, which isn't a circuit rule.
0.50 is 1/C; it still has to be inverted.

questions.prompt: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and its plates are pulled twice as far apart. What happens to the energy it stores?
questions.explanation: Disconnected, its charge Q stays fixed. Doubling d halves C, and U = Q²/(2C) doubles. The extra energy comes from the work done pulling the attracting plates apart.
choiceExplanations: Halving happens if the battery stays connected, so that ΔV is fixed.
U depends on 1/C, which only doubles here.
Changing C with Q fixed changes U = Q²/(2C).

questions.prompt: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while its plates are pulled twice as far apart. What happens to its charge and its stored energy?
choices: The charge halves and the energy stays the same
The charge stays the same and the energy doubles
questions.explanation: Connected to the battery, ΔV stays fixed. Doubling d halves C, so Q = CΔV halves and U = ½C(ΔV)² halves. The battery takes back charge as the plates separate.
choiceExplanations: U = ½C(ΔV)² halves along with C when ΔV is fixed.
A smaller C at the same voltage holds less charge, not more.
That describes a disconnected capacitor, where Q is fixed.

questions.prompt: An isolated, charged capacitor has its gap filled with a dielectric of constant κ = 3. What happens to the voltage across it?
questions.explanation: Isolated, Q stays fixed. The dielectric multiplies C by 3, so ΔV = Q/C becomes one third as large.
choiceExplanations: C changes by κ, not κ², so the voltage falls by a factor of 3.
ΔV stays the same only when a battery holds it fixed.
Voltage falls, because the same charge now sits on a larger capacitance.

questions.prompt: Why does inserting a dielectric between a capacitor's plates increase its capacitance?
choices: The dielectric increases the distance between the plates
The dielectric conducts extra charge onto the plates
The dielectric's molecules polarize, partly cancelling the field, so the plates hold more charge at the same voltage
The dielectric makes the plates larger
questions.explanation: In a field, the dielectric's molecules polarize, with their charges shifting slightly. That creates an opposing field inside, so for a given voltage the plates can hold more charge: C = κε₀A/d is larger.
choiceExplanations: A larger gap would lower the capacitance, not raise it.
A dielectric is an insulator; no charge flows through it.
The plate area doesn't change.
